item.content:encoded:
A zero-dependency plugin for effortless template and frontmatter injection

Every time I start a new file—whether it’s a new markdown blog post with Hugo frontmatter, a boilerplate Go script, or a React component—I find myself repeating the same tedious dance: copying frontmatter from another post, clearing out the old content, or searching for a boilerplate snippet.

While full-featured snippet engines exist (like LuaSnip), they often feel like overkill when what you really want is full-buffer template scaffolding. Moreover, managing heavy dependencies across multiple machines can quickly complicate what should be a minimal, snappy Neovim setup.

To solve this, I built temp.nvim: a lightweight, zero-dependency Neovim plugin designed to inject custom templates, boilerplate, and metadata directly into your buffers through an interactive prompt.

The Problem: The Boilerplate Friction

When developing across different languages or writing for static site generators, boilerplate is unavoidable:

  1. Static Site Generators (Hugo, Astro, Zola): You need precise YAML/TOML frontmatter with timestamps, slugs, and tags.
  2. Scripting (Bash, Python): You need standard shebangs, argument parsers, or if __name__ == "__main__": blocks.
  3. Configuration & Web Development: Boilerplate components, HTML skeletons, or license headers.

Snippet plugins excel at short, inline expansions, but full-file templates often feel awkward inside them. You shouldn’t need a 500-line snippet definition just to load a base file format.

I wanted something that:

  • Had zero external dependencies.
  • Utilized Neovim’s native UI elements (vim.ui.select and vim.ui.input).
  • Allowed quick creation, editing, and selection of templates.
  • Could dynamically inject contextual variables (like dates, file basenames, and titles).

Designing temp.nvim

The core philosophy of temp.nvim is minimalism and native integration. Neovim’s Lua API has matured tremendously, meaning we don’t need third-party UI libraries to build an interactive, polished experience.

1. Native UI Integration

Instead of bundling custom floating windows or demanding telescope.nvim as a strict dependency, temp.nvim relies on vim.ui.select. If you use telescope.nvim, fzf-lua, or dressing.nvim, temp.nvim automatically inherits your styled selector. If you run vanilla Neovim, it falls back cleanly to the built-in command-line menu.

-- Simplified logic behind template selection
vim.ui.select(available_templates, {
    prompt = "Select Template to Inject:",
    format_item = function(item)
        return item.name .. " (" .. item.filetype .. ")"
    end,
}, function(choice)
    if choice then
        inject_template(choice)
    end
end)

2. Dynamic Placeholders

Static templates only solve half the problem. Blog posts need current timestamps; code files need current filenames and module names. temp.nvim processes simple token replacements before inserting the template into the buffer:

  • {{date}}: Formatted ISO 8601 or custom date string.
  • {{filename}}: Base name of the current buffer.
  • {{title}}: Clean, title-cased representation of the file name.
  • {{author}}: User-configured author name.

3. Buffer-Safe Injection

A common frustration with template inserters is accidentally overwriting work in an existing buffer. temp.nvim checks if a buffer is empty or if the user explicitly triggered an append/prepend action, ensuring you never accidentally overwrite existing code.

Installation & Configuration

Installing temp.nvim with lazy.nvim is straightforward:

{
    "adnair2024/temp.nvim",
    cmd = { "TempInject", "TempNew" },
    keys = {
        { "<leader>ti", "<cmd>TempInject<cr>", desc = "Inject Template" },
    },
    opts = {
        templates_dir = vim.fn.stdpath("config") .. "/templates",
        variables = {
            author = "Ashwin Nair",
        },
    },
}

Example: Hugo Blog Post Template

Here is how simple it is to define a template. In your templates/hugo-post.toml:

+++
title = "{{title}}"
date = "{{date}}"
draft = true
tags = []
categories = []
+++

# {{title}}

Write your thoughts here...

Whenever you open a new markdown file in Neovim and hit <leader>ti, temp.nvim prompts you, parses the placeholders, and populates the buffer instantly:

+++
title = "My New Feature"
date = "2026-09-26T10:15:00-05:00"
draft = true
tags = []
categories = []
+++

# My New Feature

Write your thoughts here...

Why Build Minimal Tools?

Building temp.nvim reinforced something I appreciate about the Neovim ecosystem: the best plugins are often small, focused utilities that do one job well without imposing a massive abstraction layer.

By keeping the plugin dependency-free and adhering strictly to the vim.api and vim.ui interfaces:

  • Startup time impact is essentially 0 ms.
  • It will continue to work across Neovim versions without breaking changes from third-party libraries.
  • The codebase is easy to read, tweak, and contribute to.

If you want to streamline your workflow and stop copying boilerplate by hand, check out temp.nvim on GitHub!

item.title: Pokemon Tinkering
item.description:
Shiny Patcher: A Deep Dive into ROM Manipulation and Pattern Matching!

Building a tool to modify legacy games requires more than just changing a few bytes; it is a delicate dance of reverse engineering, memory management, and robust pattern matching. The Shiny Patcher project is a Flask-based utility designed to give players control over their Pokémon experience—specifically targeting Gen 3 (GBA) and Gen 4 (NDS) titles—by allowing custom shiny rates and event flag toggling.
item.content:encoded:
Shiny Patcher: A Deep Dive into ROM Manipulation and Pattern Matching!

Building a tool to modify legacy games requires more than just changing a few bytes; it is a delicate dance of reverse engineering, memory management, and robust pattern matching. The Shiny Patcher project is a Flask-based utility designed to give players control over their Pokémon experience—specifically targeting Gen 3 (GBA) and Gen 4 (NDS) titles—by allowing custom shiny rates and event flag toggling.

Here is the technical breakdown of how we solved the most complex hurdles during development.

Project Overview

Shiny Patcher operates as a web-based bridge between raw ROM data and user-friendly toggles.

  • Backend: Python with Flask for the web server.
  • ROM Handling: ndspy for Nintendo DS file system manipulation and standard byte manipulation for GBA.
  • Frontend: A modern, reactive interface built with Tailwind CSS, featuring a persistent Soft Reset (SR) counter stored in localStorage.

Technical Challenges and Solutions

1. Eliminating False Positives in GBA Event Flags

One of the earliest hurdles was “ghost” events. In Pokémon FireRed, the scanner initially reported that the Aurora Ticket and Birth Island events were active on vanilla (unmodified) ROMs.

The Fix: We realized the scanner was simply checking if a byte was non-zero. Since vanilla ROMs often contain junk data or different metadata at those offsets, we moved to strict validation. The patcher now specifically looks for 0x01—the exact byte our tool writes—to confirm a flag is active.

2. Solving the “Regex Parenthesis” Trap (NDS)

When searching for assembly patterns in NDS arm9.bin files, we encountered a frustrating re.error: missing ).

The Cause: In ARM assembly, the byte 0x28 represents a CMP instruction. However, in Regex, 0x28 is the ASCII code for (, which starts a capture group.

The Solution: We implemented escaped byte patterns and enabled re.DOTALL to ensure the binary data was handled as a single string of bytes.

3. Performance Optimization for HGSS

Nintendo DS ROMs (specifically HeartGold and SoulSilver) are significantly larger and more complex than GBA files. Initial versions of the patcher would hang because ndspy was decompressing and recompressing the arm9.bin file multiple times in a single request.

The Refactor:

  • Single-Pass Processing: We modified the logic to load the ROM into memory once, perform all scans and patches, and then save the final state.
  • Compression Management: By explicitly setting rom.setArm9Compression(True), we prevented the output files from bloating to massive, unplayable sizes.

Technical Specifications

GBA FireRed (BPRE v1.0)

The GBA implementation relies on “Spec-First” detection. Rather than searching the whole ROM, we check the most reliable offsets first to ensure speed and accuracy.

Feature Specification
Shiny Offset 0x39D5A (Primary), 0x39D5E (Secondary)
Assembly Pattern XX 28 01 D2 (CMP R0, #XX; BHI)
Event Flags 0x13A (Aurora), 0x8D5 (Birth Island)

Nintendo DS (HGSS IPKE/IPGE)

DS patching is more dynamic, requiring a targeted search within the ARM9 binary.

  • Search Range: 0x60000 to 0x85000 within arm9.bin.
  • Pattern Matching: 00 0C XX 28 01 D2.
  • Logic: The code looks for the LSR (Logical Shift Right) instruction, which shifts the internal ID to prepare for the shiny comparison.

Current Project Status

Shiny Patcher is now stable and highly accurate. It prioritizes hardcoded offsets for known versions while maintaining a robust fallback search for minor revisions. The UI remains lightweight, providing a scrolling marquee of supported titles and a persistent counter for hunters who prefer the long way—even if the rates are in their favor.

What’s Next? Now that the core patching engine is solid, we can focus on expanding the Event Toggle library to include Gen 3 legendary encounters like Mew on Faraway Island.
